query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, the metastable microstructure (characterized by nanocrystalline or amorphous regions) evolves during exposure to corrosive and high-temperature oxidative environments by segregating Mg to form stable intermetallic compounds at internal boundaries. This phase transformation drives changes in corrosion behavior by enhancing local galvanic coupling and concurrently improves high-temperature oxidation resistance through the stabilization of protective oxide scales.
generation.material_initial_state: As-processed, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with primarily metastable, nanocrystalline/amorphous phases and minimal intermetallic compound development.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to controlled corrosive environments and high-temperature oxidation cycles.
generation.conditions: Laboratory tests under standardized corrosion (e.g., salt spray or electrochemical testing) and oxidation (controlled high-temperature furnace conditions) regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and growth of stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds at grain boundaries and phase interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The initial metastable microstructure facilitates rapid Mg diffusion upon environmental exposure, triggering phase separation. The formation of intermetallic compounds alters local electrochemical potentials, increasing susceptibility to localized (galvanic) corrosion, while also enabling a more uniform and protective oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial state, the alloy after treatment will display increased corrosion rates (evidenced by more pronounced local galvanic corrosion) and improved high-temperature oxidation resistance (observed as a more uniform, protective oxide scale) as a direct result of the evolved microstructure.
generation.baseline: Properties measured on the as-processed metastable alloy before environmental exposure.
generation.boundary: Applicable for alloys with density below 6 g/cm³ and under exposure conditions that are sufficiently aggressive to drive phase evolution without causing complete structural failure.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative aspects of the kinetics and extent of phase transformation, as well as the precise balance between deteriorated corrosion resistance and improved oxidation resistance, remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples: one set retained in the as-processed state (control) and one set subjected to accelerated corrosion and high-temperature oxidation cycles. Characterize both sets using X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase evolution, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for microstructural changes, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) for corrosion behavior, and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) for oxidation kinetics.
measurements: XRD phase identification to quantify the formation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds
SEM imaging to assess changes in microstructure and intergranular phases
EIS and potentiodynamic polarization for corrosion rate analysis
TGA and oxide scale thickness measurements for oxidation performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, following treatment, there is no statistically significant increase in Mg-rich intermetallic compound content along with no corresponding changes in local corrosion behavior or high-temperature oxidation performance relative to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
